atoms.text: Emily Wilding Davison was an English suffragette who fought for women’s right to vote. She was born in 1872 in Greenwich to a middle-class family, became a suffragette in 1906 and quickly became known for her aggressive style of activism. She broke windows, set fire to postboxes, and, on three occasions, hid overnight in the Houses of Parliament. Emily Wilding Davison was considered a hero by thousands of people. After she died in 1913, over 5,000 suffragettes and 50,000 supporters witnessed the carrying of her coffin.

Emily Wilding Davison endured a lot of pain for her beliefs. Not only was she arrested on nine different occasions, but she also went on hunger strike seven times as a method of protest. However, she is remembered most in history for running onto the track at the 1913 Epsom Derby, where she was hit and killed by King George V’s horse. No one is really sure what she planned to do, as she kept it secret right up until her death. Some historians say she was attempting to pin a suffragette banner to the king’s horse, while it was running at about 35 mph!

After her death, Emily Wilding Davison was described by the suffragette movement as courageous and inspiring. Her death marked a turning point in the suffragette movement. In 1918, the government finally passed the first law giving women the right to vote in England.
